newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Greens iron lady Voynet gets environment.
newsitem.headline: French Greens iron lady Voynet gets environment.

text.p: Dominique Voynet, the iron lady of France's ecologist Greens, became minister of regional development and environment on Wednesday after leading her tiny party to its first seats in parliament.

The appointment to Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's cabinet rewards the 38-year old doctor who calls herself a "pretty rebellious kid" and has retained a sense of outrage at injustice in France or abroad.
Decried by opponents as vindictive and authoritarian, she is lauded by friends as a hurricane of a woman with a sharp mind who enjoys working under stress.
She will have a vital say in such issues as the future of a controversial planned Rhine-Rhone canal, the development of France's ageing fleet of nuclear power stations and motorway building.
Voynet, a single mother of two, said recently she had mellowed in motherhood but added with typically controlled aggressivity: "You must know how to smash somebody's face in."
The way she elbowed aside rivals for the leadership of the Greens party showed she had mastered the technique.
Helped by an alliance with the Socialists, her party won eight seats in the 577-member National Assembly in last Sunday's left-wing election victory.
Jospin has said his junior partners will have to bow to his line -- including a moratorium on building new nuclear power plants and cutting the work week to 35 hours from 39.

The Greens, facing an uphill battle in a country less concerned by the environment than northern European states, want to phase out nuclear power and atomic weapons, drastically raise environmental standards and cut the work week to 32 hours.

Voynet has been living in a political fast lane ever since she attended her first political demonstration at the age of 10 to protest against death sentences on Basque separatists under Spanish dictator Francisco Franco.

In the 1995 presidential election won by conservative Jacques Chirac, Voynet was the youngest candidate at 36. She won a tiny 3.3 percent after elbowing aside other ecologist rivals who disliked her overtly left-wing politics.
"She did everything early," her mother says. "She was ahead at school, she started work early, she had a baby at 19."
Voynet was born to Socialist parents,in 1958, the year General Charles de Gaulle founded France's Fifth Republic.
She worked as a night nurse to fund her medical studies and became active in the ecology movement at 18, campaigning against nuclear power.
She was a co-founder of the French Greens at 26.
Attractive, tough and fiercely independent, she once told an interviewer on a live radio programme to "P... off".
"He wanted to shine at my expense," she explained later.
As the Greens' spokeswoman, Voynet ousted party president Antoine Waechter after the divided ecologist movement failed to win a single seat in a 1993 parliamentary election.
She also outmanoeuvred former environment minister Brice Lalonde as a potential rival in the 1995 presidency race.

Voynet secured the Greens' electoral victory by creating an alliance with the Socialists. Socialist candidates stood down for Greens in 29 constituencies in return for the ecologists' support in other races to the 577-seat assembly.
